e.t: This adjective means “without a king,” describing someone or something that has no king ruling over it. It identifies the absence of royal leadership rather than naming a particular person or event. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 30:27. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and context, but its basic meaning remains the lack of a king or kingly rule.

Abia, also rendered Avia, is a proper name used for people in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies individuals rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs 24 times across 24 Old Testament verses in the Greek LXX corpus, with most occurrences found in 1 and 2 Chronicles. Its precise reference changes from passage to passage, so the surrounding verse is needed to identify which person is meant.

Agla is a proper name, referring to a person identified by that name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 3:3. The available rendering is also “Agla,” preserving the name rather than translating it into a descriptive word. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding biblical passage, but the word itself functions as a personal name.

Ada, also rendered Atha, is a personal name used for individuals in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a proper name rather than as a description of a quality, action, or object. This name occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing mainly in Genesis and once in 1 Chronicles. The supplied passages identify people by name, but no further meaning or etymological sense is established here.

This word means “choose”: to select one person, course, or thing rather than another. As a verb, it describes an act of decision or preference, whether the choice is made by an individual or expressed on behalf of others. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs nine times, so it describes a recognizable action rather than a rare technical term. The surrounding words determine what is being chosen and why; the basic idea remains deliberate selection.

This Greek LXX verb means “feel bodily pain; suffer.” It describes experiencing pain or distress, functioning as a verb for what someone undergoes rather than for an object or person acted upon. The word occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, including several uses in Job and one each in 2 Samuel, Psalms, Jeremiah, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is the experience of pain or suffering.

Amos is a proper name referring to the prophet Amos. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used as a personal name rather than as a general word describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears 20 times in this Greek Old Testament corpus, including references in 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the book of Amos. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but the word itself identifies the person named Amos.

This verb means “scream out”: to cry aloud with a strong, forceful voice. It describes an audible outcry rather than a quiet request or unspoken feeling. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 40 times, showing that it can describe people calling out in different situations. Its exact force in any passage depends on who is crying out and what the surrounding words say.

This adjective describes someone or something as unreasonable or unfair. It points to conduct or judgment that does not treat matters rightly or reasonably. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 12:26, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its core sense remains clear: a person or action marked by unfairness or a lack of reasonable treatment.

Anoun, also rendered Anun, is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object; its function is to name someone. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Nehemiah 3:13. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself establishes identity but does not provide additional information about the person or his role.

Anon is a proper name, referring to a named person or place rather than expressing a general idea or action. In the Greek Old Testament, the name appears once, in Joshua 15:50, and is rendered “Anon.” The available wording identifies the name but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain anything further about the person or place it designates. Its exact significance in Joshua 15:50 must therefore be understood from that passage’s context.

This adjective describes someone or something as “unfaithful” or “unbelievable.” It can point to a lack of faithfulness or trustworthiness, or to something that is not credible. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Proverbs and Isaiah, so it is an uncommon word in this corpus. Its exact force—whether describing a person’s character or the credibility of a matter—depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This noun means “destruction” or “waste”—the ruin, loss, or devastation of something. It can describe what has been brought to nothing or left desolate. In the Greek Old Testament, the word appears 100 times, showing that it is used broadly for destructive loss rather than for one narrow kind of damage. Its precise force in any passage depends on what is being destroyed and the surrounding sentence.

“Aroēr; Arir” is a proper name, functioning as a specific designation rather than a general word with an everyday definition. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs 17 times across 17 verses, beginning in Numbers and continuing through Jeremiah. The supplied references show it recurring in passages from Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, and other Old Testament books. Its exact referent in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Asaias (also rendered “Aseas”) is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament translation. It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs once in the LXX, in 2 Kings 22:14. The available lexical information gives the name’s identification, while the surrounding verse is needed to explain which person is meant there for the reader.

This word means “immediately,” describing something done or happening without delay. As an adverb, it modifies an action or event by showing that it follows at once rather than after a waiting period. It occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings represented here, once in Daniel and once in 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains direct and consistent: an action takes place right away.

This Greek LXX verb means “grow” or “increase.” It describes becoming greater in size, number, strength, or extent. The word can express natural growth or an increase that takes place over time, and its basic sense applies whether the subject is living, such as people or creatures, or something that expands in reach or abundance. It occurs 39 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, beginning in Genesis and continuing through 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in a particular verse comes from the surrounding sentence.

Achechar is a proper name, also rendered Akhekhar. It identifies a particular person or named figure rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, this name occurs once, in Nehemiah 3:22. The available information identifies the name and its location, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain anything further about the person or the role the name has in that passage.

The word is a proper name rendered as “Babylōnios; Vavilonios,” identifying a person or thing by that name rather than expressing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings, it occurs five times, across Ezra, Isaiah, Epistle of Jeremiah, and Bel and the Dragon. Because no verse text is provided here, its precise referent in each passage must be determined from the surrounding verse.

This adjective describes something loathsome or disgusting—an object, condition, or matter regarded with strong aversion. It expresses an intensely negative judgment about what is repulsive or detestable rather than merely unpleasant. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 41:5. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its basic meaning remains a strong description of something that causes disgust or deep revulsion.

Gadēra is a proper name rendered as “Gadēra” or “Gathira.” It identifies a named biblical entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in Joshua 15:36 and once in 1 Chronicles 4:23. Because no surrounding verse text is provided here, the precise role of the name in either passage must be determined from its immediate context.

Gebere is a proper name, referring to a specific place or location rather than expressing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Joshua 19:13, and is rendered “Gebere.” The available information identifies the name but does not provide a further definition or describe the location’s significance. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the list of places being described.

Γελβουε is a proper name for a location, rendered “Gelboue” or “Yelvue.” It is not a general word describing an object, action, or quality, but a place-name used in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs eight times, in passages from 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, and 1 Chronicles. Its exact significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic function is to identify this location.

Godolia, also rendered Gotholia, is a personal name rather than a word describing an idea, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a person in the text. It occurs four times in the Greek LXX, appearing twice in 1 Chronicles and twice in Jeremiah. Because it is a proper name, its meaning is primarily its identifying function: it points to the individual named Godolia. The surrounding verse is needed to identify which person is intended in each occurrence.

Daketh, also given as Thaketh, is the name of a specific place in the Greek Old Testament. It is a proper noun, so it identifies a place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Joshua 19:35. The available information identifies the name itself, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain more about the place or its role in that passage.

This verb means “open thoroughly/wide.” It describes opening something so that what was closed becomes accessible or visible. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 35 times. The word can describe opening a physical thing, but it may also refer to making something perceptible or accessible. Thus, its central idea is deliberate or complete opening rather than merely touching or approaching something. Its exact force in any particular passage depends on what is being opened.

This Greek LXX verb means “do”: it describes carrying out an action or deed. As a verb, it expresses what someone does rather than naming a person, object, or quality. The word occurs three times in the Greek LXX corpus, in Wisdom and 4 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains broad, so the surrounding sentence determines what action is being described in each passage. The word is found in Wisdom 14:10, Wisdom 15:6, and 4 Maccabees 11:4.

This noun means “rising,” referring to the act or movement of rising up. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Psalm 138:2. The word itself identifies an upward movement or emergence, while the surrounding verse determines its precise force there. Its basic meaning is therefore simple: a rising, whether understood as getting up or coming forth, according to the context in which it appears.

This noun means “stepping out” or “progression,” describing movement forward or an advancing course. It can refer either to the act of going out or to progress along a path, depending on the sentence. The word occurs three times in the Greek text represented here, all in Wisdom: 2:17, 8:8, and 11:14. These occurrences establish a general idea of movement or development, but the precise emphasis in any one passage depends on its surrounding wording and context.

This verb means “extend”: to make something reach outward or become longer. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it is used broadly, appearing 138 times across 133 verses. The surrounding words determine what is being extended and how the action operates in a particular passage, but the central idea remains the deliberate reaching or stretching of something outward. Its lexical sense is established by the meaning “extend.”

This verb means “show mercy” or “have mercy on.” It describes responding to someone with compassion and kindness, especially when that person is in need or distress. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scriptures, it occurs 111 times, so it is a broadly used word for merciful action rather than a rare expression. Its exact force in any passage depends on who is showing mercy and toward whom, but the central idea remains a compassionate response.

This noun means a thought or a piece of reasoning—the content formed in the mind when someone considers something. It can refer to an inward idea or line of thought, whether sound or misguided. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 28 times, appearing especially often in Ezekiel. Its ordinary sense remains focused on what a person is thinking or reasoning, while the surrounding passage determines the particular thought being described.

This adjective means “bloodless” or “drained of blood.” It describes a person, creature, or thing from which blood is absent or has been lost. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 14:46. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning remains a condition marked by the absence or loss of blood.

gl: begin with; make a beginning of
d: begin with; make a beginning of

e.t: This Greek LXX verb means “begin with” or “make a beginning of.” It describes starting an action, activity, or utterance rather than merely continuing something already underway. The word occurs 11 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, including passages in Exodus, Numbers, and 1 Samuel. Its exact sense in any verse depends on what is being started and the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains initiating or leading off an action. [p03:word:lxx:L704883:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L704883:occurrences]

This Greek LXX verb means “sit upon”: it describes taking a seated position on something or being seated on it. Its basic sense is straightforward and physical, expressing the action of sitting on a person, object, or place when the surrounding sentence identifies what is involved. It occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented here, with occurrences in 2 Samuel, Sirach, 2 Maccabees, and the Epistle of Jeremiah. The precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse.

This Greek LXX noun refers to an admonishment or a penalty—a word for corrective warning or an imposed consequence. Its basic sense covers either the act of rebuking someone or the penalty connected with wrongdoing, depending on the sentence in which it appears. It occurs once in the Greek text of the deuterocanonical book Wisdom, at Wisdom 3:10; the surrounding verse text is needed to determine which aspect is emphasized there.

Ermath is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. As a name, it identifies a particular person or place rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. Its exact referent cannot be determined from the lexical information alone. Ermath occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Joshua 12:14, so its meaning is essentially the name itself rather than a broader recurring concept.

This noun means “redness on the skin,” describing a visible reddened area of the body. It refers to a physical skin condition rather than an action, person, or character quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 63:1. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary lexical sense remains a red appearance or discoloration on the skin.

This adverb means “easily,” describing something done without unusual difficulty or hindrance. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Proverbs 30:29. As an adverb, it modifies an action or description by showing the manner in which something proceeds. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense is straightforward: something happens readily, smoothly, or without great effort.

gl: furnish with supplies for a journey
d: furnish with supplies for a journey

e.t: This Greek Old Testament verb means to furnish someone with supplies for a journey. It describes providing what travelers need for their road, especially food or other provisions. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in Deuteronomy and once in Joshua. Its basic sense is practical and generous: making sure a person is equipped for travel rather than sending them away empty-handed.

This noun refers to “lewdness” or “loose conduct”—behavior marked by shameless moral looseness rather than ordinary restraint. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament represented by the Septuagint, at Judges 20:6. Because the lexical sense is brief and the verse text is not included here, the word’s exact force in that sentence must be understood from its surrounding passage. Its central idea remains conduct viewed as indecent and morally unrestrained.

This adjective describes something as “full of life” or “lively.” It can point to vitality, animation, or a quality marked by living energy rather than dullness or lifelessness. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Wisdom 15:11. Its exact force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning describes what is alive, vigorous, or animated.

This word means “half,” referring to one of two equal parts of a whole. As a noun, it identifies a portion divided from the complete amount. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all in Numbers 31, where the term describes portions resulting from a division. Its central meaning remains straightforward: one part of something split into two equal shares. The surrounding passage determines what is being divided, but the word itself expresses the portion, not the act of dividing.

Thamar is a personal name identifying a woman in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a common word describing an object, action, or quality, but a name used to distinguish this person in the biblical family and genealogical record. The name occurs eight times in seven verses, appearing mainly in Genesis 38 and also in Ruth, 1 Chronicles, and related Old Testament genealogical material. Its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding verse and its place in the person’s story.

This word means “spectator”—a person who watches or observes rather than taking the central action. It is a noun referring to someone present as an onlooker. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 4:19. The word’s basic sense identifies a witness or viewer, while the surrounding verse would determine the particular situation and emphasis. Its meaning remains distinct from the action or event being observed.

Ieththor is a proper name, referring to a named individual rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 1 Samuel 30:27. The available lexical wording identifies the name as “Ieththor,” but does not provide an additional meaning or English rendering. Its specific identity and role must therefore be determined from the surrounding passage.

This verb means to make something adequate or sufficient. As a verb, it describes an action that brings something to the needed measure, so that it is enough for its purpose or need. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 14 times in 14 verses. The word therefore focuses on making adequacy present, rather than merely declaring that something is adequate. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This noun refers to venom, a poisonous substance that harms or kills, and can also describe corrosion—the damaging effect that eats away or destroys. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs ten times, showing use for both a literal harmful substance and destructive decay. Its central idea is something dangerous that works injury, whether pictured as poison within a creature or as a force that wears something down. The surrounding verse determines which sense is intended.

This word means “fish,” referring to an aquatic creature. It is a noun used for fish as part of the created animal world and as food or living creatures found in waters. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 25 times across 23 verses, from Genesis through Zephaniah. Its uses include fish associated with humanity’s rule over living creatures and fish affected by the waters of Egypt. The basic meaning remains direct and concrete: a fish or fish collectively, depending on the sentence.

This adverb means “exactly as,” marking a close comparison between one action, statement, or situation and another. It points readers to something already mentioned or understood and says that the present matter corresponds to it precisely. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used broadly rather than being limited to one subject or kind of event. The word occurs 78 times in the Greek LXX corpus, including passages from Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Joshua, and the deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in a particular sentence comes from what it compares.

This verb describes something that has been cobbled or clouted—fitted with patches or coverings, especially in connection with footwear. It points to an object made serviceable by adding or fastening material rather than being new or intact. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Joshua 9:5. The exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself emphasizes patched, repaired, or roughly covered condition.

This verb means to boast—to speak with pride about oneself, one’s strength, or an achievement. It describes the act of making something a reason for confidence or self-exaltation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 32 times, showing a recurring biblical concern with what people proudly rely on or proclaim. The word can describe human boasting, while Scripture also presents God as the one whose power makes human boasting empty. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

This word is a proper name, referring to someone identified as “Kinaios” or “Kineos.” It functions as a personal or family name rather than a general description, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs seven times across five verses, all in Judges and 1 Samuel. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise identity in each occurrence cannot be stated more specifically, but its basic role is naming rather than describing.

This verb means “exhausted” or “labor”: it describes working hard, becoming weary, or being worn down through effort. In the Greek Old Testament, it can refer both to the activity of laboring and to the resulting exhaustion. The word occurs 50 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, so its basic idea is broadly used rather than limited to one particular situation. The surrounding passage determines whether the emphasis falls on strenuous work, weariness, or both.

This noun can mean “world” or “adornment.” It may refer broadly to the created world, or to something arranged, decorated, or made beautiful. The surrounding sentence determines which sense is intended, so the word should not be limited to only one English idea. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 66 times, with both meanings included in its lexical range. It appears from Genesis through 4 Maccabees, including a rendering as “world” in Genesis 2:1.

This Greek LXX verb means “hit” or “light upon”—to come upon something or someone by striking or reaching it. It describes an action rather than a person, place, or quality. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 7:9. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its precise force in that occurrence must be understood from its context. Its central idea remains an encounter or contact expressed as an active verb.

This is a proper name or designation for a Levite. It identifies a person belonging to the Levitical group in the Greek Old Testament, rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The word appears 274 times in the Greek Old Testament, so it is a regularly used designation across that corpus. Its precise reference in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

Maasēa, also rendered “Maasia,” is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in Ezra and once in Nehemiah. The name identifies a person in each passage, but the available text here does not establish whether both references concern the same individual. Its precise reference therefore depends on the surrounding passage.

Mareth is a proper name, identifying a person or place rather than expressing an ordinary action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears only once, in 1 Chronicles 4:17. The available wording identifies the name as “Mareth,” but no further meaning or description is provided here. Its specific identity and significance therefore depend on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included in this word-level entry.

Machemas is a proper name, rendered “Machemas” or “Makhemas.” It identifies a particular named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs nine times, with most occurrences in 1 Samuel and single occurrences in 1 Kings and Nehemiah. Because the available information gives the name but not the verse wording or surrounding context, its precise referent and role must be determined from each passage.

This adjective describes something as “magnificent” or “glorious”—splendid, impressive, and worthy of honor. It expresses a quality of greatness or majesty rather than naming an action or person. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 5:8. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what it describes there, but its basic sense points to something distinguished by splendor and grandeur.

This verb means to moderate or keep measure—to act with restraint rather than excess. It describes measured conduct and can express the idea of maintaining a proper limit. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 2:2. Since the verse text and surrounding context are not available here, the word’s exact force in that sentence cannot be expanded beyond this central sense. Its meaning points to controlled, balanced action rather than something extreme.

“Moodi” is a personal name, also rendered in the gloss as “Moothi.” In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a particular person rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. The name appears once, in Ezra 10:34. Because the surrounding verse text is not provided here, the name itself does not establish anything further about that person or his circumstances.

This adjective describes someone who is blamed or held at fault. It points to a person regarded as responsible for wrongdoing or deserving accusation, rather than simply describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Deuteronomy 32:5. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense is a negative description of a person considered blameworthy.

This word is a proper name rendered “Naid” or “Neth.” It does not function as an ordinary descriptive word such as a noun, verb, or adjective; rather, it identifies a named entity in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs once in the LXX, at Genesis 4:16. The supplied lexical meaning gives only the name itself, so identifying the specific person, place, or other referent requires the verse text and its surrounding context.

Naphisōn, also written Nafison, is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs once, in Ezra 2:50. Because a proper name identifies someone rather than describing a general idea or action, its meaning is chiefly the person designated by that name. The surrounding verse is needed to explain who Naphisōn was and what role he had in that passage.

This noun refers to emotion—the inward feeling or stirring of the heart. It names what a person experiences internally rather than an outward action. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 30 times, so it is a recurring word for describing human inner life. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains emotion.

This Greek LXX noun means “hewing,” referring to the work of cutting or shaping wood. It names an activity rather than expressing a command or describing a feeling. In the Septuagint’s Old Testament Greek corpus, it occurs five times, in Deuteronomy and Joshua. The word points to practical labor involving hewing, while the surrounding verse determines exactly how that labor is being mentioned.

This Greek LXX adjective describes someone connected with a household, or something belonging to the house. It can refer to a household member and carries the idea of being part of one’s own household rather than an outsider. The word occurs 19 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus. Its precise wording in English depends on whether it describes a person or something associated with the house.

This adverb means “unanimously” or “with one accord,” describing people acting, speaking, or responding together in unity. It emphasizes shared purpose and agreement rather than merely being present at the same time. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 27 times, including passages from Exodus, Numbers, Job, Jeremiah, Wisdom, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains collective agreement and united action.

This noun means “unripe grape,” referring to fruit that has not matured. It names a grape in its early, undeveloped state rather than a fully ripened fruit. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times across six verses, including passages in Job, Proverbs, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains an immature grape not yet ready for full ripeness.

This Greek LXX noun means “pulse,” referring to a kind of food. It is a specific name for food rather than an action, quality, or person. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in Daniel 1:12 and Daniel 1:16. Its basic meaning remains simple and concrete: pulse as a food item. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain how the word functions in either particular passage.

This word means “serpent,” referring to a snake or similar creeping creature. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings to name such an animal. The word appears 39 times in this LXX corpus, including passages in Genesis, Exodus, and Numbers. Its meaning remains the ordinary name for a serpent; any particular significance in a passage must come from that passage’s surrounding words and events.

This Greek LXX verb means to treat with distinction—to distinguish one person, group, or thing from another. It describes recognizing or showing a meaningful difference rather than treating everything alike. The word occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented in this corpus, including several passages in Exodus. Its exact force in a particular sentence depends on what is being distinguished and how the surrounding passage describes that difference.

Patrosōniim, also rendered Patrosonim, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person or people in the Greek Old Testament, but the available wording does not provide enough surrounding context to say more about who they were or what role they had. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Genesis 10:14. Its precise significance there must be understood from the surrounding passage.

This noun means “thickness,” referring to how thick something is from one side to the other. It describes a measurable physical dimension, especially in references to constructed objects or materials. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 12 times, including several descriptions connected with temple furnishings and building details. The word’s basic sense remains physical rather than figurative in the available information.

This adjective means “fifty years old,” describing a person’s age. It identifies someone who has reached the age of fifty, rather than naming an occupation, status, or personal quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs seven times, all in Numbers, where age is specified in connection with people being counted or assigned for service. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: the person described is fifty years old. The surrounding wording determines how that age functions in each passage.

This noun means “perch,” referring to a place or support where something can rest or sit. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Proverbs 9:18. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not available here, the word’s precise role in that verse cannot be described further. Its basic meaning remains a perch: a resting place or support, rather than an action or quality. This is a distinct Greek LXX word, preserved here in its Old Testament setting.

e.h: A Word for Many Times Over
e.t: This word is an adjective that describes a quality or condition. Its basic sense is “many times over”. It points to something multiplied or greatly increased rather than present only once. In the Greek LXX material, it appears one time, in 2 Maccabees 9:16. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the adjective itself emphasizes repeated or abundant increase. It is therefore a word of strong multiplication, describing something that exists or happens many times over.

This Greek LXX noun means “putting to” or “application”—the act of bringing something into contact with or applying it for a purpose. It names an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX, both times in 2 Maccabees, so its normal sense is established by a small number of uses. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This verb means “stick to; bond,” describing close attachment or joined commitment. It can express the act of holding closely to someone or remaining firmly connected. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 16 times, so its central idea is recurring rather than limited to one passage. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and subject.

This verb means to travel near or approach someone or something. It describes movement toward a person or place, rather than simply remaining nearby. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 17 times, mostly in Old Testament books. Its use in passages from Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers reflects ordinary physical movement toward a designated person or place. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is drawing near or coming toward.

This verb means to inquire—to seek information by asking—or to ascertain something by finding out what is true or known. It describes an active effort to gain information, rather than merely possessing knowledge. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 12 times, including uses across Genesis, Chronicles, Esther, Daniel, and other books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being investigated and how the surrounding sentence presents the inquiry.

Ram, also rendered Rham, is a proper name used for a person in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies individuals in genealogical records and in Job, rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name appears four times in the Greek Old Testament, in three verses in 1 Chronicles and once in Job. Its meaning here is therefore chiefly identification: Ram is the personal name by which a particular man is distinguished from others in the biblical record.

This verb means to “bring into measure”: to make something fit a measured or proportioned standard. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Isaiah 44:13. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central meaning remains the act of bringing something within measure or proper proportion.

Samaōth, also rendered Samaoth, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person named in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 27:8. Since the available material gives the name but no further explanation of its origin or significance, its secure meaning is its identity as a personal name. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain the person’s specific role there.

e.h: Able to Quench or Put Out
e.t: This adjective describes something able to quench or put out, especially something that can extinguish what is burning. It presents the quality or capacity to stop a flame or similar force rather than naming the action itself. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), this word occurs once, in Wisdom 19:20. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning is the ability to extinguish or suppress.

This word means “moon,” the visible heavenly body that marks the night sky. It is a noun used for the moon itself, including its appearance, position, or place among the lights of heaven. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings, it occurs 38 times, showing a consistent and straightforward meaning across its uses. The word appears from Genesis through Song of Songs, including passages that mention the moon alongside the sun or other heavenly bodies.

Sechonias is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is also rendered Sekhonias, reflecting the same name rather than a separate meaning. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX, in 2 Chronicles 31:15. Because it is a personal name, its meaning is primarily identification: it tells the reader who is being mentioned, rather than describing an action, quality, or object.

This noun refers to the vertebrae—the individual bones that make up the backbone or spine. It is a specific anatomical term rather than a word for the whole body or skeleton. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 10:8. The available lexical meaning identifies the word clearly, while the precise force of the term in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text.

This noun means “inscription” or “title”—a written heading placed with a psalm or other text. It refers to identifying words attached to a composition, rather than to the main body of the composition itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, all in the Psalms, including headings associated with Psalms 15, 55, 56, 57, 58, and 59. Its basic sense is therefore a written designation that introduces or identifies what follows.

This verb means “joint heir; heir with,” describing someone who receives an inheritance together with another person. It presents shared heirship rather than inheritance held alone. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Sirach 22:23. Because the verse text is not included here, the word’s precise role in that sentence depends on its surrounding context; its central meaning remains participation in an inheritance alongside someone else.

This word means “Syēnē” or “Sini”. It is a proper name, referring to the place-name used in the Greek text of Ezekiel. The word appears three times in the Greek Old Testament, all within Ezekiel: once in chapter 29 and twice in chapter 30. These occurrences use the same named location rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The precise significance of the place in each passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This verb means “wrestle with,” describing a struggle or contest involving another person or opposing force. It presents the action of contending rather than simply meeting or accompanying someone. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical books, it occurs three times: once in Genesis and once each in Sirach and Baruch. Its exact force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains active struggle or contention with something or someone.

This verb describes acting as a “shield-fellow”—someone who stands together with another in shared defense or combat. It presents the action of joining another’s protection, like companions forming a united shield line. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 3:10. Since the verse text is not included, the surrounding passage would determine exactly how this shared defensive action is expressed there.

e.t: This noun refers to the healing of a wound, including the forming of a complete scar as the injury closes and recovers. It describes the result or process by which damaged flesh becomes healed rather than remaining an open wound. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, at Jeremiah 40:6. Its basic sense is therefore specific: the restoration of a wound to a healed condition, marked by complete scar forming.

This adjective describes something likely to make a person stumble. It points to a quality that can cause someone to lose steady footing or go astray, depending on the surrounding sentence. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 5:6. The word therefore carries a focused sense of danger or instability rather than describing something firmly secure. Its exact force in that verse must be understood from the surrounding passage.

Sobab is a proper name, rendered as “Sōbab” or “Sovav.” It identifies a particular person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, the name occurs three times: once in 2 Samuel and twice in 1 Chronicles. Because the name appears in genealogical and royal-family records, its meaning is chiefly identifying—the word points to the individual named Sobab. The surrounding verse is needed to explain that person’s specific role in each occurrence.

Tabaōth, also rendered Tavaoth, is a proper name rather than a descriptive word. It identifies Tabaoth in the Greek Old Testament text, appearing twice: once in Ezra and once in Nehemiah. Because names normally identify people, families, or groups rather than express an action or quality, its meaning is best presented as the name itself, not translated into an English concept. The surrounding verse text would be needed to identify exactly whom or what Tabaoth designates in each occurrence.

This Greek LXX adjective means “on the third day” or “three.” It expresses a number or identifies something connected with the third day, depending on how it functions in the sentence. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in 1 Samuel 9:20. Its basic meaning is therefore numerical or time-related, while the surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on the number three or on the third day.

This verb means to delight oneself or live softly—that is, to enjoy ease and comfort rather than hardship. It describes a way of living marked by pleasure or settled well-being. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 9:25. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is enjoying a comfortable, pleasurable life.

This Greek LXX verb means to “leave below/behind”—to leave something or someone remaining, or to be left behind after others have gone. It describes an action rather than a person or object, so its exact sense depends on what is being left and the surrounding sentence. The verb occurs 80 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, showing a recurring idea of something remaining behind or being left over.

This Greek LXX verb means “elevate” or “lift up.” It describes raising something physically, bringing it upward, or exalting it to a higher position. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 170 times, so its basic sense appears across many kinds of passages rather than belonging to one narrow setting. The surrounding words determine whether the lifting is literal or figurative, but the central idea remains movement or placement upward. It is found throughout the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books in this Greek corpus.

Phoinissa is a proper name, also rendered Finissa. It identifies a named individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Septuagint, this name occurs once, in Exodus 6:15. Its meaning is therefore chiefly its identification of the person bearing the name; the surrounding verse supplies the person’s specific place in the genealogy. This is a Greek LXX name and should be understood within that Greek Old Testament corpus.

Chalannē (also rendered Khalanni) is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in Genesis 10:10 and once in Isaiah 10:9. The lexical meaning supplied for the name is simply “Chalannē; Khalanni,” so its precise referent must be determined from the surrounding verse and passage. It should therefore be read as a name, not translated as an ordinary descriptive term.

This word means “of winter,” describing something associated with the winter season. It is an adjective, so it normally characterizes a person, thing, condition, or time as belonging to or relating to winter. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, each in a different verse. Its use is therefore focused and specific rather than broad: it identifies a seasonal connection, not a general quality. The precise force in any one passage depends on the noun or situation it describes.

This verb means “contribute”: it describes taking part by giving something toward a need, work, or shared purpose. It presents contribution as an action, rather than as a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 17 times across 16 verses, showing that it can describe this kind of participation in various settings. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This word means “Anointed.” It functions as a noun or adjective, identifying someone or something associated with anointing. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books represented here, it occurs 43 times, with 41 occurrences in the Old Testament and 2 in Deuterocanonical books. Its repeated English rendering is “anointed,” confirming this as its ordinary lexical sense. The word appears across legal, historical, and poetic books, while the surrounding passage determines whom or what it describes.

This word means “song,” referring to words joined with melody or singing. It is a noun used for a composed or performed song, especially in passages connected with worship, celebration, or public praise. In the Greek Old Testament and related writings, it occurs 78 times, with many occurrences in the Psalms. Its use reaches from the song recorded after Israel’s deliverance in Exodus to songs associated with worship and gathered praise. The word itself identifies the song, while the surrounding passage determines its particular subject and purpose.
